source: Schmalhofer and Polson (1986) A production system model for human problem solving (Experiment 1)
finding: Tested whether people keep a fixed noticing order of moves (the assumption in the Jeffries et al. 1977 means-ends model). Showing all legal moves in a means-ends order, or in a different means-ends order, did not change behaviour in river-crossing problems. A fixed internal noticing order is not supported.
numbers: 120 students, 3 groups of 40 (two display orders, one control). (5,3) task, legal moves mean (SD): 27.85 (29.74), 27.88 (27.23), 27.10 (28.90). Repeated-measures ANOVA: no significant differences, all F < 1. Move-transition correlations between control and each display group above .95. The text says the Jeffries model could not fit the (5,3) problem without 'baroque ad hoc assumptions'.
quote: could not be accounted for by this model without introducing baroque ad hoc assumptions
limits: Secondary account of Jeffries et al., not the 1977 paper. Student sample, one lab. OCR of the tables is partly garbled, so use the means with care. The experiment shows the noticing order is not needed; it does not show that people never use means-ends.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one fixed order for trying operators. Let the order follow the current state (what is shown or ledgered), not a stored list.

source: Schmalhofer and Polson (1986) A production system model for human problem solving (model, Experiment 2, ablations)
finding: A model that fits three river-crossing problems mixes two strategies that are not integrated: means-ends move generation (move travellers toward the goal bank) and a 'balance' strategy that satisfies the outnumbering rule. A probability decides which one fires. Moves are checked by an 'avoid backward move' rule and a subgoal-protection rule, but the subgoal 'all missionaries on the goal bank' is only recognised after it is accomplished. Removing the balance strategy breaks the harder problems, where highly unbalanced states must be visited.
numbers: Experiment 2: 120 new students, 40 per problem, (3,2), (4,3), (5,3). Legal moves observed 16.55 / 18.90 / 28.25, model 17.34 / 18.54 / 27.37; state-transition correlations .98 / .93 / .94 (illegal-move correlations at least .90 with one general parameter set). Ablation, mean moves (correlation) for (3,2)/(4,3)/(5,3): without balance production 18.02 (.94) / 15.74 (.76) / 32.22 (.78); without subgoal protection and level-2 means-ends evaluation 26.04 (.74) / 19.20 (.84) / 36.78 (.84); without long-term storage of visited states 23.94 (.87) / 22.57 (.91) / 34.19 (.90).
quote: the balance and the means-ends strategies are not integrated into a coherent mental representation
limits: Simulation of group means, not individual protocols. Parameters fitted. Table 8 is garbled in the OCR; row labels were matched to the text. Student puzzle solving, not expert work.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete picture of non-greedy moves: means-ends alone is not what people run. A second, constraint-driven move generator, a memory of visited states, and a check that avoids undoing the last move were each needed. Build these as separate slots next to difference reduction.

source: Greeno (1974) Hobbits and orcs: acquisition of a sequential concept (abstract as shown in search results)
finding: Abstract-level only (the repository page returned 403 and the journal text is paywalled). Subjects solved hobbits-orcs repeatedly until two errorless solutions. Results support organisation of moves in small subsequences, oriented forward, which differs from the retroactive organisation of GPS on this problem. Learning fits all-or-none acquisition at individual states, with one exception tied to ambiguity about backward moves.
numbers: No sample sizes or error rates read.
limits: NOT OPENED. Summary taken from a search result. Do not use numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Still a pointer. The forward-subsequence result suggests chunking short move runs as one unit, not a pure goal stack.

source: Thomas (1974) An analysis of behavior in the hobbits-orcs problem, Cognitive Psychology 6, 257-269 (citation and secondary summaries only)
finding: Not opened (paywalled). Greeno's companion abstract says it gives further support for Thomas's conclusion that subjects organise moves in small subsequences. A low-authority study site says Thomas argued that solvers must temporarily move away from the goal state.
numbers: None read.
limits: NOT OPENED. The move-away-from-goal reading comes from a flashcard site and must not be used as evidence.
agent_relevance: The detour claim for hobbits-orcs is still second-hand. Gap 4 stays open at the primary-paper level.

source: Jeffries, Polson, Razran and Atwood (1977) A process model for Missionaries-Cannibals and other river crossing problems, Cognitive Psychology 9, 412-440 (abstract only)
finding: Abstract-level only. Extends the Atwood and Polson (1976) water-jug model to four isomorphs of Missionaries-Cannibals. Cover story left legal moves to solution unchanged but caused large differences in illegal moves. A three-stage model (means-ends heuristics, memory use, illegal-move detection) accounts for legal and illegal moves in all four versions.
numbers: None read.
limits: NOT OPENED. The fit was for the (3,2) problem; Schmalhofer and Polson (d01, d02) report it failed on (5,3) without ad hoc assumptions.
agent_relevance: Isomorph wording changes errors, not path length. Argues for a restated, neutral problem representation (S0-S2) to cut illegal moves.

source: Levin, Riel, Cohen, Goeller, Boruta and Miyake (1987) Reflexibility in problem solving: the social context of expertise (missionaries and cannibals part)
finding: Single solvers of missionaries-cannibals moved pieces with no evaluation, planned on the fly, rarely proposed then considered a move, and ended with no memory of the solution path because of many incorrect or backward moves. Pairs had to justify moves, which led to reflection on whether a move brings the solvers closer to the goal; the second person monitored illegal moves and lack of progress; when stuck, pairs more often restarted from the beginning.
numbers: 10 individuals and 10 pairs, 11-step solution. Single solvers 13.30 min vs pairs 7.09 min; 27 vs 17 moves; repeat moves 40.2% vs 22.4%; illegal moves 1.2% vs 0.08% as printed.
limits: Tiny sample, no statistics in the part read, transcripts coded by the authors. Social context, not a model.
agent_relevance: A forced justify-the-move-against-the-goal step plus a monitor role cut repeat moves by almost half. Restart from the start is a human version of a sanctioned non-greedy reset.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking, latest HTML version with responses to critics
finding: Reasoning models beat non-reasoning models only at medium complexity and both collapse beyond. Giving the Hanoi algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse. The authors answer critics: the first Hanoi failure comes early (about move 40 of 255 at N=8; within the first 100 moves at N about 10), not at the end, so context limits are not the cause; temperature 0 changes nothing; they removed N above 12 for Hanoi and restricted River Crossing to N below 6.
numbers: Hanoi collapse for reasoning models at N=7-8 (about 100-200 moves). First failure: N=8 about 40 moves (15% of 255); N about 10 about 100 moves (10% of about 1000). Hanoi N=12 failed below 50 moves while N=10 succeeded past 100 (non-monotone). River Crossing N=3 (11 moves) already collapses. Equal-token pass@k: thinking and non-thinking models comparable on MATH500, but three regimes on puzzles. DeepSeek-R1 at temperature 0 collapses in Blocks World at N=4, with sampling at N=30.
quote: even when we provide the algorithm in the prompt
limits: The Apple authors' own reply to critics, so not neutral. Many claims are shown as figures, not tables. The algorithm-given result is on Hanoi and Checker Jumping only.
agent_relevance: A model that must execute a long algorithm by itself still errs early even with the algorithm in hand. The design should not rely on the model to apply a known procedure across hundreds of steps; code should.

source: Su, Li, Marques, Flint, Zhu and Dev (2025) Limits of emergent reasoning of LLMs in agentic frameworks for deterministic games
finding: Gave the model a Hanoi environment: one move per tool call, environment holds and returns the state, invalid moves blocked, full move history shown. This did not remove collapse; collapse began at lower disk counts than in one-shot output. Failures were deterministic loops: the model reused the same continuations.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet (thinking and not) and DeepSeek V3.1 / R1; up to n=8 disks; token budget 30,000. About 40% of the time the model deterministically reuses earlier continuations at n=8. Jensen-Shannon divergence from the optimal policy and from the random policy both rise with n.
limits: Preprint by a student research group. One run per setting, no repeated trials, two model families, only up to 8 disks, no temperature or voting ablation (authors' own limitations). No algorithm in the prompt, so the model must also find the strategy.
agent_relevance: Putting state in code is not enough. The agent needs a loop detector (state already visited) and a forced different choice, or voting across independent samples. This supports a visited-state guard in the scaffold.

source: Rethinking the Illusion of Thinking (2025) stepwise resolution and agentic dialogue on Hanoi and River Crossing
finding: Re-ran Hanoi by asking for p moves at a time from the current state; both a single reasoning model and a two-model dialogue with shared memory still fail consistently from about N=8. Two-agent dialogue was worse (struggles from N=4) and kept spending tokens in legal but unproductive cycles. River Crossing on solvable instances only was solved well, even N=100 with k=4; the hardest cases were N=4-5 with k=3.
numbers: Hanoi N=3 to 10, 10 trials per setting. River Crossing k=2 to 4, N=2 to 100, 10 trials each. The original paper's rates were read from plots, so comparisons are approximate.
limits: Preprint, 10 trials, model not named in the text I read, original numbers approximated from figures. Authors say they will scale up later.
agent_relevance: Splitting the output does not remove the hard part at about 8 disks. The River Crossing collapse was mostly invalid instances. Do not read either as a general law; the failure depends on task and format.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER), full text re-read
finding: The 20-disk Hanoi was actually run, not only projected: gpt-4.1-mini, one step per agent, the solving strategy given in every prompt, current state given, first-to-ahead-by-k voting (k=3), outputs over 750 tokens discarded as a red flag. The run finished with zero errors. The per-step error rate is small but not zero and did not rise with disk count.
numbers: 2^20 - 1 = 1,048,575 steps. Single-step error rate on 10K random steps: gpt-4.1-mini 0.0045, o3-mini 0.0017, gpt-4.1-nano 0.3583 (as read from the Figure 6 legend). Two independent gpt-4.1-mini runs at temperature 0.1 on the 10K sample shared no step that was wrong in both. One step needed 18 voting rounds. The paper says its work covers execution, not insights.
quote: relatively small non-reasoning models are comparable to more advanced reasoning models
limits: The authors give the algorithm in every prompt, so the model only executes. Voting cost dominates. This corrects the earlier claim K23: it was a completed run, not a projection. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: For the Shojaee versus Lawsen dispute this settles the narrow point: with state supplied, one step per call, the algorithm in the prompt and voting, long Hanoi runs are error-free. The collapse is a long-chain error accumulation issue, fixable by short steps plus voting. It does not show that the model can find the strategy.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas and Sohrabi (2024, v3 2026) Thought of Search: planning with language models through the lens of efficiency
finding: Instead of having the model search, GPT-4 wrote the successor-state function and the goal test as code, and a standard BFS or DFS did the search. This solved every instance in four benchmark sets with a few model calls, and kept soundness and completeness.
numbers: 24 game: 1,362 instances, 100%; mini crosswords: 20 games; BlocksWorld: 502 instances of 4-5 blocks, all 502 solved by all 5 generated function pairs; PrOntoQA: 4,000 instances. The paper estimates that calling the model inside the search for the Blocksworld baseline would cost over $1,000.
limits: Domains are small and fully specified; the generated code sometimes needed human or test feedback to fix mistakes (the paper says the same mistakes repeat across runs). Larger BlocksWorld would cost more for the search too.
agent_relevance: Best fit for puzzles and planning items with a clear goal test: the model supplies the transition rules and the goal check once, code does the goal-difference search. For items with no clear goal state this route is closed.

source: Prasad, Koller, Hartmann, Clark, Sabharwal, Bansal and Khot (2024) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with language models, ablations re-opened
finding: Beyond the main table, ADaPT was run with GPT-4, LLaMA-2 70B and Lemur 70B too, not only GPT-3.5. Raising the maximum decomposition depth helps in steps. On WebShop the always-decompose baseline (static decomposition) did worse than the plain executor, while as-needed decomposition did better than both.
numbers: Depth cap dmax 1, 2, 3 on ALFWorld, WebShop, TextCraft (dev splits): performance rises with each step; 1 to 2 gives the largest jump. TextCraft test by recipe depth: depth 2 ReAct 26.9 vs ADaPT (dmax=4) 78.2, mean depth used 1.9; depth 3 ReAct 1.8 vs 38.7, depth used 2.8. ADaPT improves GPT-4 by up to 37 points on TextCraft (figure only). WebShop (Table 7): iterative executor 29.0 success, static decomposition 17.0, retry 30.0, Reflexion 35.0, ADaPT 44.0. ALFWorld with the Yao et al. executor (test): ReAct 56.7, plan-and-execute 63.4, Reflexion 67.2, ADaPT 79.8. LLaMA-2-70B executor alone 20.4, with a GPT-3.5 planner 43.3 (dev).
limits: 2023 models. GPT-4 numbers only as a figure. Cap of 4 never pushed higher. Does not test current reasoning models or thinking on. Cost shown in LLM calls, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Supports decomposing only after a failed attempt, with a depth cap near 3, and shows blanket decomposition can hurt. Whether this survives current models is still unmeasured.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: the decreasing value of chain of thought in prompting
finding: Asking for step-by-step reasoning helped non-reasoning models a little on average, but added variability and sometimes lowered perfect accuracy. For reasoning models (o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5) the prompt gave little or no gain and cost more time.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, 25 trials per question per condition. Reasoning models: only o4-mini at the 51% metric gained (+5.6 points, p=.003); Gemini Flash 2.5 lost 13.1 points at 100%-correct and 7.1 at 90%. CoT requests took 20-80% (10-20 s) longer for reasoning models. Non-reasoning: Sonnet 3.5 +10.1 points (100% metric); Gemini 2.0 Flash -13.1 (100% metric) but +13.6 (51% metric).
limits: A one-line think-step-by-step prompt, not a structured scaffold. One benchmark, multiple-choice science QA, not planning. Not a test of means-ends.
agent_relevance: Indirect evidence for gap 1: prompt-level reasoning structure adds little once a model reasons natively. A means-ends scaffold with a code-held ledger could still differ, but this predicts small gains and a risk of hurting. Test with thinking on before shipping.

source: Wang, Min, Deng, Shen, Wu, Zettlemoyer and Sun (2022) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting: an empirical study of what matters
finding: Prompts with logically invalid reasoning steps kept 80-90% of the CoT benefit, but removing relevance to the query or coherence of step order removed most of it. The model still produced sound reasoning on the test item.
numbers: InstructGPT text-davinci-002; GSM8K (800 test items) answer accuracy: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid reasoning 39.5, no coherence 23.1, no relevance 11.0 (below standard). Bamboogle (125 items) answer F1: standard 20.6, CoT 45.2, invalid 39.4, no relevance 23.9.
limits: 2022 model, two tasks, hand-written invalid rationales kept relevant and in order. Not planning; not a difference-operator table.
agent_relevance: Nearest evidence on gap 5. A scaffold hint that is wrong in logic but relevant and well ordered costs about 20% of the gain. A hint irrelevant to the item can be worse than none. So a badly named difference is probably tolerable; one that points at the wrong objects is not. Still untested for operator tables.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam and Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of large language models on reasoning and planning tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own answers made accuracy fall; with a sound external verifier accuracy rose, and the content of the critique mattered little (plain re-prompting kept most of the gain). As a verifier GPT-4 produced many false negatives, so it rejected correct answers.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Standard / LLM+LLM self-critique / sound verifier with binary feedback: Game of 24 5% / 3% / 36%; Graph Coloring 16% / 2% / 38%; Mystery Blocksworld 4% / 0% / 10%. Sampling 25 times with no critique: 42%, 44%, 14%. LLM verifier: Game of 24 accuracy 87.0%, false positive 10.4%, false negative 20.7%; Graph Coloring 72.4%, FP 6.5%, FN 95.8%; Mystery Blocksworld 79.6%, FP 0.5%, FN 97.09%.
limits: GPT-4 from early 2024, three domains, no reasoning model. The paper says the verifier requires high accuracy but gives no number.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model act as its own progress checker for subgoals. A code check (state recomputed from the ledger) is needed; and plain resampling already gets most of the gain, so test subgoal checks against resampling at equal tokens.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song and Zhou (2023) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking the model to review and revise its own answer did not help and often hurt. Reported gains in earlier work came from using the correct answer to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard / self-correct round 1 / round 2: GSM8K 75.9 / 75.1 / 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 / 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 / 25.0 / 25.0. GPT-4 standard: GSM8K 95.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0, HotpotQA 49.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 / 88.0 / 90.0.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction with a generic prompt; models of 2023; no reasoning models. A different checker design could do better.
agent_relevance: Same direction as d15: a model that checks its own progress without an outside signal is unreliable, even when it is capable of the task.

source: Huang, Lipovetzky and Cohn (2024) Chasing progress, not perfection: revisiting strategies for end-to-end LLM plan generation
finding: A rare separate test of a goal-distance part and a state part. Fine-tuned Qwen2-7B planners were given either Goal CoT (repeat the goal and count the steps left) or State CoT (write the conditions and effects of each action). Goal CoT did not help on out-of-distribution sets and was the only strategy that hurt; State CoT raised executability (100% on the unseen set) but not on longer plans. Self-correction training detected wrong steps well but did not raise validity.
numbers: PlanBench-style data, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, fine-tuned. Mistake detection with all four strategies: precision 90.5%, recall 99.2%, yet validity rates did not improve. Authors' reasons for Goal CoT failing: estimating goal distance adds a task and locks the plan length; the model's numbers stay near training plan lengths.
limits: Fine-tuned small model, not prompted frontier models. Goal CoT here counts remaining steps; it is not difference naming. No token-matched baseline.
agent_relevance: First direct hint on gap 2: counting distance to goal can hurt, while stating exact state and effects helps within the trained length range. Argues for a ledger first, and for treating any distance-to-goal estimate as risky unless code computes it.

source: Thinking forward and backward: effective backward planning with large language models (2024), re-opened
finding: Backward planning in the model is worse than forward on average, but flipping the problem (goal becomes start) then planning forward removes that bias. Combining forward and flipped candidates with self-verification raised planning success by 4 to 24 points. Self-verification quality depends on model strength; GPT-3.5 accepted every Blocksworld plan.
numbers: 200 trials per setting, up to 6 attempts. In one array-transformation setting Fwd vs Back 53.5% vs 36%, Fwd-Flip vs Fwd-Back 56% vs 46%. The model chose the easier direction 78.5% of the time on undirected graphs and 60.5% on directed graphs. GPT-3.5 in Blocksworld always judged its own plan correct, giving close to zero success.
limits: GPT-4o and older models, three simple domains, self-verification not external. One setting where all baselines were near 100% showed no gain.
agent_relevance: Confirms K17 from the paper text. The GPT-3.5 accept-all verifier is a clean example of false progress being accepted; use it as a guard test for any model-run subgoal check.

source: Query-efficient planning with language models (2024)
finding: Stepwise, goal-directed ReAct-style agents got stuck in cul-de-sacs and loops (pick up a block, put it back down) and tended to attend to recent history. A generative planner that proposes a whole action sequence and resets to the start after feedback escaped. A one-shot prompt that fixed the action description and repeated the goal beat ReAct by 12.3 and 14.8 points.
numbers: Blocksworld, Logistics, Grippers, Robotouille PDDL benchmarks. Mean tokens per run: I/O about 0.5k, I/O+CoT about 1k, Boomerang about 38k, ReAct about 51k. Boomerang was the most query-efficient on 100 examples each of Logistics, Grippers, Robotouille.
limits: Prompted older GPT models, small domains, success curves shown as figures not tables.
agent_relevance: A greedy step-by-step loop with full history repeats states. A sanctioned reset to the start state is an effective non-greedy move. Repeating the goal at each step is cheap and helped.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried and Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: A memory of reusable workflows induced from earlier tasks helped web agents. Memory learned offline from a training set lost its edge as the gap to the test set grew (new website, new domain), while memory induced online from the test stream did not.
numbers: WebArena (gpt-4): 51.1% relative success gain over the baseline (12.0 points). Mind2Web cross-task step success: 24.6% relative gain. Cross-website and cross-domain, online AWM 8.9 to 14.0 points above baseline, margin widening with the train-test gap. Gain over baseline up to 22.5 points after tens of examples.
limits: Web navigation, not planning puzzles. Induced workflows are action sequences, not control rules. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: The Prodigy lesson holds: stored control knowledge helps most when it matches the current problem class. Prefer memory induced inside the current run or class, and expire it when the class changes.

source: Zhao, Huang, Xu, Lin, Liu and Huang (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Natural-language insights plus retrieved successful trajectories raised success on three task types. Insights taken from HotpotQA and rewritten with a few target examples transferred to FEVER, a neighbouring task with the same tool.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 actor. HotpotQA: insights-only 36%, retrieval-only 31%; ALFWorld: 50% and 55%. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER (success %): Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer without target demos 65 (std error 1.7), with target demos 70 (0.7).
limits: Source and target share the Wikipedia tool and question style. Gains of 2 to 7 points over ReAct. No far-class transfer, and no test where a wrong rule is stored.
agent_relevance: Near transfer works with a rewrite step. This does not show transfer across problem classes, so memory needs a class tag and a retire rule.

source: Li and Kingsford (2026) MEDAKA / LiquidWorld, ablation and setup re-read from the HTML
finding: Re-reading the ablation shows what the two arms are. '- Recursive Module' keeps per-step tracking with all numeric computation instructions as an algebra-aware CoT. '- State Tracking' keeps recursive goal decomposition but drops the per-step tracking and all numeric computation instructions. Each arm alone recovers more than half of the full gain over CoT. Thinking mode was turned off for all models by design, and external solvers or verifiers were left out on purpose.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.6: CoT 77.8, full 94.5, no state tracking (decomposition only) 90.5, no recursive module (tracking only) 91.0, so decomposition alone recovers 12.7 of 16.7 points (76%) and tracking alone 13.2 (79%). Gemini 3 Flash: CoT 65.6, full 82.0, no tracking 76.0, no recursion 75.1: 10.4 of 16.4 (63%) and 9.5 (58%). Nonlinear tag, full / no state / no recursive: Claude 87.4 / 82.4 / 83.0; Gemini 50.9 / 36.5 / 28.9. Coupling (Gemini): 68.9 / 58.2 / 56.0.
limits: Two models, one synthetic domain, 3 trials. The state tracking arm bundles the ledger with numeric calculation instructions, so a pure ledger or pure stack arm still does not exist. No arm isolates difference naming. Shares are my arithmetic from the published table.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is half answered: the stack and the tracking-plus-calculation module are each worth most of the gain and the two overlap. No evidence on difference naming. Build ablation arms that separate ledger, calculation hints, stack and difference naming.
